title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 9: Civil Society's Role in Promoting Democracy and Development
keywords: Civil Society's Role in Promoting Democracy and Development
Asian Institute of Management Policy Center
William Easterly, Elusive Quest for Growth
poverty as deprivation of essential assets and opportunities
primary_topics: Chapter 9 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- his lecture to the Asian Institute of Management's 51st Globalization Lecture Series, the first time he was asked to correlate his judicial philosophy of Liberty and Prosperity with civil society's role in economic development, argued throughout from the perspective of the judiciary.

A restatement of the philosophy itself: the four Ins, the plague of 'ships,' the four ACID problems and the revitalized bar as means toward the two loftier goals of safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity while upholding the rule of law and judicial independence.

Civil society's stake and standing: a pillar of democracy, the conscience of government and the overseer of governmental actions that in fact precedes the judiciary as the vanguard of freedoms, operating within the Bill of Rights and bounded by the line between legitimate protest and destabilization.

Three concrete ways civil society can promote economic development by supporting judicial initiatives -- initiating cases and causes, pushing legal empowerment of the poor, and advocating collective cooperation against poverty.

The claim that the battle for liberty and prosperity is finally a battle for the poor and the marginalized, since freedom and political equality are meaningless to people wallowing in grinding poverty, and that human dignity requires both.
sub_topics: His opening joke that his wife Leni's 32-year stint on the AIM faculty exerts a tectonic influence over him, so that this once he must succumb to influence.
The three-part plan of the lecture: a brief disquisition on Liberty and Prosperity, civil society's stake in this egalitarian philosophy, and specific ways it can contribute.

The vow on assuming office on December 21, 2005: four Ins, moral courage against influence, interference and indifference, imperviousness to kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship, and the four ACID problems.
The Supreme Court's mandate over the bar, 'the vineyard from which our judges take root,' and the renaissance of a competent and ethical legal profession.
Courts as the great equalizers between citizens and government, most urgently when individual freedoms confront the awesome powers of the State.
Civil liberties specified: inviolability of persons and homes against arbitrary searches and seizures, freedoms of abode and travel, and Miranda rights -- a never-ending saga of trials and triumphs.

His observation that lawyers' knowledge of civil liberties is negatively correlated with how little they have devoted to nurturing prosperity, despite constitutional mandates on the marginalized, a just and dynamic social order and equitable distribution.

The constitutional prosperity mandate addressed to all three departments, and his quotation from his own book Leveling the Playing Field on integrity, stability and predictability of decisions and on safeguarding not only food but also freedom.
Poverty redefined as a 'deprivation of essential assets and opportunities to which every human is entitled,' elevating the right to prosperity to a universal human right.

The long Philippine tradition of citizen associations and the recent recognition of civil society's power, with its full roster from self-help groups and neighborhood associations to PVOs, NGOs and sectoral aggroupments.

Civil society at the forefront of the fight for liberty: bringing down a dictatorship and rejecting a later administration perceived as corrupt, carving 'People Power' into the citizenry's consciousness.
Its non-political work: basic social services, grassroots organization, conflict resolution, and training in human rights, gender equality and credit and debt repayment.

The legal framework: Bill of Rights guarantees of speech, association, assembly and information; the constitutional mandate of participation at all levels of policymaking; and tax exemptions and ODA funds granted to CSOs, POs and NGOs.
The limits: respect for fair comment, privacy and disclosure, and the line between legitimate protest and unlawful mass actions, interference and destabilization.

The round-table with Professor William Easterly, Secretary Margarito Teves, former Prime Minister Cesar Virata, Felipe Medalla, Senator Ralph Recto, Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala II, Alex Magno, Reza Bagir and Joaquim von Amsberg, concluding that no single international formula ensures rapid growth.
His Philippine argument from experience: Martial Law proved authoritarian rule incapable of meaningful long-term progress, and Filipinos will not exchange their freedoms for food.

Donor agencies redirected toward accountable, rule-based institutions: the UNDP's four supported lines of work on access to justice for the poor, the World Bank and ADB on good governance as a prerequisite to growth, The Asia Foundation's Philippine and Mindanao programs, and USAID and national aid agencies on anti-corruption.

Cardoso's June 2004 report for the UN Panel of Eminent Persons on public opinion as a key policy factor and the broadening from representative to participatory democracy, in which citizens aggregate in communities of interest rather than electoral districts.

The three supporting roles: initiating judicial proceedings with help from the IBP, PBA and FLAG; the ADB-commissioned study's three legal-empowerment recommendations; and advocacy for collective solutions to poverty, exemplified by the Gates Foundation and Bono.
His closing reiteration of the clarion call to the business community to espouse jobs and justice, food and freedom, investments and integrity, economics and ethics, development and democracy.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduced Chief Justice Panganiban's lecture to the Asian Institute of Management Policy Center's 51st Globalization Lecture Series, an invitation he said he could not decline because of his wife Leni's 32-year stint on the AIM faculty. It was, he noted, the first time he had been asked to correlate his judicial philosophy with civil society's role in economic development, and he divided the lecture into a disquisition on Liberty and Prosperity, civil society's stake in it, and the specific ways it could contribute. He restated the vow he made on December 21, 2005 -- a judiciary of four Ins, impervious to the plague of 'ships,' battling the four ACID problems -- and the Supreme Court's supervision of the bar, 'the vineyard from which our judges take root,' with both directed to safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity. Observing that lawyers' mastery of civil liberties has not been matched by attention to prosperity, he cited the Constitution's prosperity mandates and quoted his own book Leveling the Playing Field, and argued that the redefinition of poverty as a deprivation of essential assets elevates the right to prosperity to a universal human right. Turning to civil society, he traced its long Philippine tradition, credited it with People Power and with services, organizing and training beyond politics, and called it a pillar of democracy that precedes the judiciary as vanguard of freedoms -- while insisting its participation is bounded by the same Constitution that sustains it, since anarchy destroys both liberty and prosperity. He reported a round-table with Professor William Easterly and Philippine economic officials that found no single formula for growth, yet maintained that Martial Law had proved authoritarianism barren and that Filipinos would not trade freedom for food. He surveyed the reorientation of UNDP, World Bank, ADB, Asia Foundation and USAID programs toward access to justice and anti-corruption, cited Cardoso's panel on participatory democracy, and closed by naming three roles for civil society: initiating cases, pushing legal empowerment of the poor, and advocating collective solutions to poverty.
